en: The bones of my limbs cracked;
Truly, I have been grievously wounded.
The moon is dark and the night is thin;
What will become of us at night
If the swine attacks the exhausted?
What will become of us by day?
My arms hang numb and palsied;
Thinking of it leaves the head bewildered,
And the mind scattered among countless cares.
Sixty sorrows and a thousand ordeals
Appear close before my brow.
I find no people to stand behind me,
No lion to join me in combat;
I have neither musket nor support.
What manner of encampment will remain
For my diminished Kyrgyz people?
The noble Kyrgyz in their white kalpaks
Have broad pastures and open roads.
When the khan desired, they slaughtered sheep,
And prepared feasts for all the people.
What fate will befall
My blessed nation?
He shook and bowed his head:
Let us look to my blood-conquering uncle,
My hero, the support at my waist,
My mighty and seasoned lion.
If I send Akjoltoy before him,
He will lead troops as countless as hosts.
With my father, the blue-maned lion,
They spurred on like yearling colts,
Contended while nursing at the breast,
Sliced fat meat and ate the mane,
And ate rich butter with cream.
They had been companions from infancy,
And those who departed grew to maturity;
Their clans had settled there from the beginning,
With inexhaustible treasure,
And possessions beyond measure.
My gallant uncle Külchoro
Stands grievously wounded;
His power is spent, his strength gone,
And my joyous people are in mourning.
Death takes many forms, all different;
Solitude differs, and so does every man.
God the Creator fashions His servants,
Each in a different way.
My first forefather Manas was a lion,
Whose strength had no equal in the world.
Yet He made his descendants feeble,
And made mankind weak;
Almighty Allah in His power
Made mankind frail—
What varied mortals He created!
Sarybay is mighty in courage,
That hideous boar.
He turned fortified folk to blood;
Can I devise a means against him,
Avenge myself upon that cunning lion,
And take vengeance on that son of a bitch?
Before him, shouting,
My heroic father, like a prophet,
Would invoke Manas as his battle cry,
Commanding, ‘Gather the scattered treasure!’
My wounded soul would rejoice,
My brow would open like the dawn,
The grief within my belly would disperse,
My aching places would be soothed,
The foe I faced would be defeated,
The ruthless enemy overcome.
My grief would scatter and vanish,
My brow would open like the dawn,
And the ancient enemy be defeated.
Will the day ever come when death is gone?
When the people rest calmly, free of turmoil,
Will the day ever come when we may lie at ease?
Will the blue-lynx and sable cap
Ever sway again in celebration?
With the people freely singing laments together,
Oh, my dear one, will a day of joy
Ever come?”
Thus Seytek stood grieving,
While the people cried out, their hearts bleeding,
Lamenting and raising a clamor.
The mighty maiden, daughter of Kayypchal,
The maiden who stirred turmoil throughout the world,
Was extraordinary in bravery,
And unmatched in strength.
Her immeasurable valor,
Throughout the whole wide world,
Had surpassed even that of lions.
Gentle in nature and pure in heart,
She was a healer and a sage,
Whose eyes could see afar.
Her figure was like a radiant sun,
A graceful and beautiful maiden.
She combed her hair like a parrot’s plumage,
And was born as white as the moon;
No other soul like her had arisen among humankind.
The hair down her back billowed softly,
Like the down on an owl’s legs.
Her figure rose tall and stately,
Like the sacred Night of Power.
Your champion had a warrior’s frame,
An immeasurably mighty wrestler.
That peerlessly born hero
Looked solemn without smiling,
And wore a silver-mounted quiver.
The radiant, graceful woman
Had a face illuminated like the sun.
No ill-fated one like her existed in the world,
Her nature unique, her face like the moon.
Her words were ardent and deeply alluring,
Her bearing unique, her eyes like a camel calf’s,
Her luminous face softly glowing,
Her bosom broad, her chest expansive.
Beautiful and dark-eyed,
Such was Kuyaly to behold.
Her gentle nature was plain to see;
It seemed she would grant my every wish.
It seemed she had been born mighty,
With valor, courage, and a radiant face—
The Almighty Lord
Had bestowed these without measure.
Her dignity was rare and pearl-like,
Her form like a maiden made of light.
Without so much as a smile, she stood solemn,
Her calm deliberation evident;
Whenever one saw her judgment,
A mortal soul entrusted to God rejoiced.
The lion-maiden wrestler’s
Character revealed itself thus:
She strode behind them, solemn,
And the poor woman of camel-like stature
Had her moonlike face bathed in light,
Her heroism plain to see.
She donned her battle armor;
The mighty maiden, fitted for war,
Destroyed whoever approached her,
And went forth to win the great prize.
Her arms were exceptional, her fury fierce;
She laid her mortal enemies low.
Her heroism became renowned,
And enemies who faced her recoiled.
Those who coveted her were slain,
And many reins were pulled tight.
Thinking, “I shall take the maiden,”
Many wrestlers and many warriors
Fell prostrate when they faced her.
Thinking, “I shall mow them like spring grass,
I shall subdue their noble people,
And slaughter their proud nation.”
Their heads were ensnared in suffering;
Eighty champions and eighty companies,
And multitudes came out to clash.
They had wrestlers and warriors,
And Sarybay stood among them;
They had champions and lions,
Lions who had thrown the whole world into turmoil.
Blustering with swollen lungs,
Their arrogant breasts pounding,
Sarybay attacked.
Heroes fell and khans died;
Through the wretched villain’s great savagery,
All who faced him perished.
Sarybay himself was wounded,
And many others came to grief.
It became a great and dreadful calamity,
A deafening uproar.
This was the maiden’s battle;
She fell into death-dealing hands.
Sarybay, son of the monster,
Had his head split seven times,
And was stabbed through seven layers.
Clouds gathered in the sky;
He raged madly as he neared death—
Such was his measure when beheld.
They entered a grievous conflict,
Fighting through summer and winter,
Wrestling and accusing each other,
Passing their days in spear combat.
Fierce in wrath was Sarybay;
Kuyaly, daughter of Kayypchal,
Showed such prowess as a wrestler.
With the warrior son of the monster,
With the lion who greased the earth with blood,
She grappled like a white snake,
And they mauled each other like ravenous stallion camels.
They had struggled against each other before;
When the infidel son of the monster
Was still young, she had encountered him.
She wrecked his camp and seized his plunder,
Slaughtered his khan and left him sprawled,
And waged a terrible battle.
She had slaughtered his people,
And divided his treasury.
She wiped out those who wore braids,
And enslaved all she encountered;
She reduced the topknotted to ashes,
And whenever enemies came to fight,
She hunted them down and destroyed them.
She threw down those lacking sense,
And many times before had made the swine
Suffer torment at her hands.
Against the hero Sarybay,
She followed close upon his yellow trail,
And stretched him out like one struck by wasting sickness.
Driving the charging warriors before her,
Kuyaly, daughter of Kayypchal,
Raged onward upon Jeljetpes;
She donned her armor for war,
Her companions swelling into a mighty host,
And whoever approached was struck down.
Blood flowed from her grappling,
And dust rose wherever she challenged.
Early words became late deeds;
Her two eyes seemed to become four.
On an earlier occasion,
When they had met face-to-face,
And gone forth to raise battle,
They stood pummeling each other,
Until they came to binding hands.
She had inflicted utter calamity
Upon Sarybay.
She bound the strong arms of
Sarybay’s countless host and blocked their open road;
Around that infidel Sarybay,
She cast a ring about his feet,
Waging a daylong battle for his blood,
Striking once more at his life.
When the struggle reached its fiercest,
Seytek brought forward a special force
And compelled them to submit.
A mighty battle and tremendous uproar—
Such was the clash they waged.
But Sarybay
Was an extraordinarily powerful weather-worker;
Rain poured over every ridge,
Hail beat upon every hollow,
Fog covered the open plain,
And fierce winds and creeping mist
Closed in and blinded every eye.
Clouds gathered across the sky;
Sarybay led Kuyaly astray
And escaped from her,
Barely saving himself from death.
Your bellowing champion,
To wage battle against the full-armed infidel,
And go forth to strike him,
Gathered her strength for a desperate assault;
To stand as a warrior on the field,
The lion-maiden Kuyaly
Chose and donned a pale-gray robe,
And mounted the swift steed Jeljetpes.
Composed yet fierce for combat,
The mighty maiden cast her life aside
And girded on a naked sword.
